abstract: |
  Deciding which industries to overweight is a ranking problem: the level of the market does not matter, only which sectors will beat the others. I rank the 49 Kenneth French value-weighted US industry portfolios every month from January 1980 to August 2026 with thirteen methods, from single signals (momentum, reversal, value) to ridge, lasso, random forests, gradient boosting and neural networks fed twelve industry characteristics and five market-state variables, using only data available at the time. The models do rank industries: the average rank correlation between forecast and next month's relative return is 0.04 to 0.05, with Newey–West t-statistics of 3 to 4.6. But the simplest rule, last year's return skipping the latest month, achieves 0.044, and no machine-learning model improves on it significantly (the largest gain in rank correlation is 0.006, t = 1.1). The skill is concentrated in momentum, collapsed after 1999 (rank correlation 0.07 in 1980–1999, 0.02–0.04 since) and is expensive to trade: a portfolio long the top ten industries and short the bottom ten earns a net Sharpe ratio of 0.16 to 0.36 after 20 basis points per unit traded, and little at 40. The skill is a long-standing anomaly, not a new machine-learning discovery.

def table(df: pd.DataFrame, fmt: dict) -> Markdown:
    d = df.copy()
    for c, f in fmt.items():
        d[c] = d[c].map(lambda v, f=f: "–" if pd.isna(v) else f.format(v + 0.0).replace("-0.0", "0.0"))
    return Markdown(d.to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))

# The question

Allocators rarely choose between "the market" and cash; they choose between sectors. A sector tilt wins if the industries held outperform the ones left out, whatever the market does. Academic evidence says the winners are partly predictable: industries that did well over the past year tend to keep doing well (Moskowitz and Grinblatt 1999), and machine-learning studies of individual stocks report large gains from combining many characteristics non-linearly (Gu, Kelly and Xiu 2020). This study asks how much of that survives at the industry level, in real time, and after trading costs.

# Design

The design was fixed before any out-of-sample result was computed. All thirteen methods are reported.

**Universe and target.** Kenneth French's 49 value-weighted industry portfolios, monthly returns, July 1926 to August 2026. At the end of each month the target is every industry's return over the next month *minus the average industry return that month*, so models are scored only on their ability to rank.

**Characteristics (12).** Each is ranked across the 49 industries every month and rescaled to the interval $[-0.5, 0.5]$ (Gu, Kelly and Xiu 2020), which removes outliers and the level of the market.

| Group | Characteristic |
|---|---|
| Momentum and reversal | Return over the last 1, 3, 6 and 12 months; the last 12 months skipping the latest (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993); months $t{-}35$ to $t{-}12$ (long-term reversal); the 12-month return relative to the market |
| Risk | 12-month volatility and downside volatility; 36-month market beta |
| Value | Book-to-market, and book-to-market relative to the industry's own five-year average |

Book-to-market for fiscal year $Y$ is used from July of year $Y+1$, six months later than strictly needed.

**Market-state variables (5).** Market volatility (log realised variance of the month), the market's 12-month return, the 10-year minus 3-month term spread, the excess bond premium and the Baa spread. They let characteristics matter more or less in different markets. A state variable enters only once it has ten years of history in the training window (the excess bond premium from 1983, the term spread from 1992, the Baa spread from 1996).

**Methods.**

| Group | Method | Specification |
|---|---|---|
| Single signals | Momentum | Last 12 months skipping the latest (12–1) |
| | Momentum (6 months), reversal, value, value relative to own history | One characteristic each; reversal is minus last month's return |
| Linear | OLS | 12 characteristics, pooled across industries |
| | Ridge, lasso, elastic net | Characteristics plus all 60 characteristic × state interactions; penalties by time-series cross-validation |
| Non-linear | Random forest | 200 trees, leaves of at least 300 industry-months |
| | Gradient boosting | Depth 3, early stopping |
| | Neural network | Two hidden layers (32, 16), average of 3 seeds |
| Combination | Average | Of the standardised forecasts of ridge, lasso, elastic net, forest, boosting and network |

**Forecasting.** Forecasts for every month-end from January 1980 to August 2026 (559 months with an outcome) use an expanding window starting in 1940. At forecast date $t$ a model learns only from rows whose next-month outcome is known (dates up to $t-1$). Linear models are re-estimated every 12 months and their penalties, with the non-linear models, every 36.

**Evaluation.** The *information coefficient* (IC) is each month's Spearman rank correlation between the forecast and the realised relative return across the 49 industries; its average measures ranking skill and its t-statistic uses Newey–West errors. The *portfolio* goes long the ten highest-ranked industries and short the ten lowest, equal-weighted, rebalanced monthly, with 20 basis points of cost per unit traded. Sharpe ratios are compared with the Jobson–Korkie test with Memmel's (2003) correction. Alphas come from regressions on the Fama–French market, size and value factors, so the alpha of a momentum portfolio includes its momentum exposure.

# Results

## The scoreboard

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scoreboard
#| tbl-cap: "Ranking skill and long-short portfolios, January 1980 – July 2026. IC: mean monthly rank correlation (Newey–West t in brackets). Portfolio: long top 10, short bottom 10 industries, net of 20 bp per unit traded. R²_OS: against a zero relative-return forecast."
b = board.reset_index()
b["IC (t)"] = b.apply(lambda r: f"{r['Mean IC']:.3f} ({r['IC t-stat']:.1f})", axis=1)
b["Alpha (t)"] = b.apply(lambda r: f"{r['Alpha (% p.a.)']:.1f} ({r['Alpha t-stat']:.1f})", axis=1)
table(b[["Model", "IC (t)", "Gross return (% p.a.)", "Net return (% p.a.)", "Sharpe, net", "Annual turnover", "Alpha (t)", "R²_OS (%)"]],
      {"Gross return (% p.a.)": "{:.1f}", "Net return (% p.a.)": "{:.1f}", "Sharpe, net": "{:.2f}", "Annual turnover": "{:.0f}", "R²_OS (%)": "{:.2f}"})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
Bd = board
ml = ["ols", "ridge", "lasso", "enet", "rf", "gbm", "nn", "mean_ml"]
best_ic = Bd.loc[ml, "Mean IC"].idxmax()
best_sh = Bd.loc[ml, "Sharpe, net"].idxmax()
```

Five results.

*The skill is real.* The linear models, the forest, boosting and the network all rank industries better than chance, as does momentum: for the eight machine-learning methods the mean IC lies between `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'Mean IC'].min():.3f}"` and `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'Mean IC'].max():.3f}"`, with t-statistics of `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'IC t-stat'].min():.1f}"` to `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'IC t-stat'].max():.1f}"`, and the rank correlation is positive in `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'Months IC > 0 (%)'].min():.0f}"`–`{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'Months IC > 0 (%)'].max():.0f}"`% of months. An IC of 0.05 is small: it is the correlation between a forecast and next month's return, and next month's relative return is mostly noise.

*Almost all of it is momentum.* The 12–1 momentum rule alone has an IC of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['mom', 'Mean IC']:.3f}"` (t = `{python} f"{Bd.loc['mom', 'IC t-stat']:.1f}"`). The best machine-learning model by IC (`{python} N[best_ic]`, `{python} f"{Bd.loc[best_ic, 'Mean IC']:.3f}"`) improves on it by `{python} f"{Bd.loc[best_ic, 'IC minus momentum IC']:.3f}"` (t = `{python} f"{Bd.loc[best_ic, 't-stat']:.1f}"`), and none of the eight is significantly better (all |t| below 1.1). The variables the forest relies on, in @fig-importance, are the momentum measures. Value is worthless at this horizon (IC `{python} f"{Bd.loc['value', 'Mean IC']:.3f}"`).

*Last month's winners keep winning.* The short-term reversal signal, minus last month's return, has a significantly negative IC of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['rev', 'Mean IC']:.3f}"`: at the industry level, one-month returns persist rather than reverse, the opposite of the pattern for individual stocks and a feature already documented by Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999). It is also the worst portfolio in the table (net Sharpe `{python} f"{Bd.loc['rev', 'Sharpe, net']:.2f}"`) because it turns the whole book over each month.

*Non-linearity does not add.* Boosting and the network do worse than the lasso, the forest only marginally better, and the out-of-sample $R^2$ of every model is at most `{python} f"{Bd.loc[ml, 'R²_OS (%)'].max():.2f}"`%: the models put the right industries on top without predicting the size of the moves.

*The portfolio is modest.* The lasso earns `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Net return (% p.a.)']:.1f}"`% a year after costs at a volatility of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Volatility (% p.a.)']:.0f}"`%, a Sharpe ratio of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Sharpe, net']:.2f}"` and an alpha of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Alpha (% p.a.)']:.1f}"`% (t = `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Alpha t-stat']:.1f}"`) against the three Fama–French factors, against `{python} f"{Bd.loc['mom', 'Sharpe, net']:.2f}"` for plain momentum. The difference between the two Sharpe ratios has a one-sided p-value of `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'p (Sharpe, net > momentum)']:.2f}"`: suggestive, not conclusive.

## The skill faded

```{python}
#| label: tbl-periods
#| tbl-cap: "Ranking skill and net long-short Sharpe ratio by period"
p = sub.copy()
p["IC (t)"] = p.apply(lambda r: f"{r['Mean IC']:.3f} ({r['IC t-stat']:.1f})", axis=1)
p["Net return (% p.a.)"] = p["Net return (% p.a.)"].map("{:.1f}".format)
p["Sharpe, net"] = p["Sharpe, net"].map("{:.2f}".format)
Markdown(p[["Period", "Model", "IC (t)", "Net return (% p.a.)", "Sharpe, net"]].to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
P = sub.set_index(["Period", "key"])
lasso40 = costs[(costs["key"] == "lasso") & (costs["Cost (bp per unit traded)"] == 40)]["Sharpe, net"].iloc[0]
```

Ranking skill was strongest in 1980–1999 (IC `{python} f"{P.loc[('1980–1999', 'mom'), 'Mean IC']:.3f}"` for momentum, `{python} f"{P.loc[('1980–1999', 'lasso'), 'Mean IC']:.3f}"` for the lasso) and has since fallen by more than half, to `{python} f"{P.loc[('2000–2012', 'lasso'), 'Mean IC']:.3f}"` in 2000–2012 and `{python} f"{P.loc[('2013–2026', 'lasso'), 'Mean IC']:.3f}"` since 2013, with t-statistics between 1 and 2. In 2000–2012 plain momentum lost money after costs (`{python} f"{P.loc[('2000–2012', 'mom'), 'Net return (% p.a.)']:.1f}"`% a year) and the machine-learning models earned only 1–3%. The models partly adapt to this (the lasso and the forest, trained on all history, held up better than momentum in 2000–2012), but the main message is that the signal weakened, in line with the usual pattern of anomalies fading after they become known (McLean and Pontiff 2016), although these data cannot tell that explanation from chance.

## Costs

```{python}
#| label: tbl-costs
#| tbl-cap: "Net return (% a year) and Sharpe ratio of the long-short portfolios for different trading costs"
c = costs.copy()
c["Net (Sharpe)"] = c.apply(lambda r: f"{r['Net return (% p.a.)']:.1f} ({r['Sharpe, net']:.2f})", axis=1)
cp = c.pivot(index="Model", columns="Cost (bp per unit traded)", values="Net (Sharpe)")
cp = cp[[0, 10, 20, 40]]
cp.columns = [f"{k} bp" for k in cp.columns]
Markdown(cp.reset_index().to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

The portfolios turn over `{python} f"{Bd.loc[['mom', 'lasso', 'rf', 'mean_ml'], 'Annual turnover'].min():.0f}"`–`{python} f"{Bd.loc[['mom', 'lasso', 'rf', 'mean_ml'], 'Annual turnover'].max():.0f}"` times their gross exposure a year, so costs decide the outcome. Before costs the lasso's Sharpe ratio is `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Sharpe, gross']:.2f}"`; at 20 basis points per unit traded it is `{python} f"{Bd.loc['lasso', 'Sharpe, net']:.2f}"`; at 40 it is `{python} f"{lasso40:.2f}"`. Industry futures or low-cost ETFs make 10 basis points plausible for an institution; 40 is closer to what a retail investor pays.

# The current ranking

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ranking
#| tbl-cap: "The five highest- and five lowest-ranked industries at the end of August 2026 by the average of the machine-learning models. Higher score: expected to beat the other industries next month. A model output with the track record above, not a recommendation."
top = cur.head(5).assign(Position="Highest ranked")
bot = cur.tail(5).iloc[::-1].assign(Position="Lowest ranked")
x = pd.concat([top, bot])
x["12–1 momentum rank"] = x["mom"].map(lambda v: f"{v + 0.5:.0%}")
x["Score"] = x["Score"].map("{:.2f}".format)
Markdown(x[["Position", "Industry", "Score", "12–1 momentum rank"]].to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

The ranking leans towards the technology hardware and metals industries and away from apparel, paper and medical equipment, which is mostly a statement about the last twelve months of returns. The score is a ranking, not a forecast of size: the best model explains under 0.2% of the variation in relative returns.

# Conclusion

Machine learning finds the industry momentum that finance already knew about. Thirteen methods, five market states and twelve characteristics rank industries with an average rank correlation of about 0.05, a small and statistically solid number, but a one-line momentum rule gets 0.044 of it and no model improves on that significantly. The skill was concentrated in the 1980s and 1990s, and after 20 basis points of trading costs the best long-short portfolio earns a Sharpe ratio of 0.36.

For an investor the use is a modest tilt, held for years rather than traded monthly, that gives up little when implemented through momentum itself. The more general lesson is the one that recurs across these studies: in noisy financial data, flexible models mostly add variance, and the benchmark worth beating is the simple rule that practitioners already use.

**Limitations.** The portfolios are value-weighted industries as defined by Kenneth French, not tradable funds, and returns are before taxes and shorting costs. The alphas control for the market, size and value but not for a market-wide momentum factor, which is why the momentum portfolio shows a positive alpha. Book-to-market is annual. Kenneth French reconstitutes the industry portfolios each June. Results rest on one market.
